statement: For small swings, a pendulum's period T = 2π√(L/g) depends only on length and g, not amplitude or bob mass.
analogy: A bigger swing is a longer lap run faster, so lap time stays the same.
steps: Restoring force ≈ -mg(x/L) for small angles
Divide by m: acceleration = -(g/L)x, mass cancels
This is SHM with ω = √(g/L)
So T = 2π√(L/g): no amplitude, no mass
worked_example: L = 1.0 m, g = π² m/s²: T = 2π√(1/π²) = 2.0 s, for a 3° or 6° swing, light or heavy bob.
verify_flags: TODO_VERIFY
Amplitude independence holds only for small angles (sinθ ≈ θ); exact period grows slightly at large angles.
O3-R contrasts with spring-mass T = 2π√(m/k), where mass does matter.

statement: For small swings, the period does not depend on amplitude.
wrong_idea: If I pull it further, it has more distance to cover, so one swing takes longer.
why_it_feels_right: Walking a longer distance normally takes more time.
why_wrong: Pulling further also gives a bigger restoring force, so the bob moves faster. For small angles the extra speed exactly makes up for the extra distance.

statement: Bigger and smaller small swings take exactly the same time per oscillation.
wrong_idea: The bigger swing goes faster at the bottom, so it finishes first.
why_it_feels_right: You can see the wide-swinging bob whizzing past faster.
why_wrong: It is faster, but it also has a longer path. For small angles speed and distance both scale with amplitude, so the time per swing stays the same.

wrong_idea: A heavier bob changes the period, it swings faster or slower than a light one.
why_it_feels_right: Heavy things feel harder to move, and for a spring a heavier mass really does slow it (T = 2π√(m/k)).

statement: In SHM, speed peaks at the mean, acceleration peaks at the extremes, and total energy stays constant.
analogy: Like money shifting between wallet and pocket: the split changes, the total doesn't.
steps: v = ω√(A² − x²) is zero at the extremes.
a = −ω²x is largest at the extremes.
KE and PE trade places.
E = ½kA² everywhere.
worked_example: m = 0.5 kg, k = 50 N/m, A = 0.1 m: ω = 10 rad/s; extreme a = 10 m/s², mean v = 1 m/s; E = 0.25 J throughout.
verify_flags: TODO_VERIFY
Concept-card worked example: ω = √(50/0.5) = 10 rad/s, v_max = ωA = 1 m/s, a_max = ω²A = 10 m/s², E = ½kA² = 0.25 J.

statement: At the extreme, velocity is zero but acceleration is maximum, ω²A, toward the mean.
wrong_idea: It stops at the end, so the acceleration there must be zero.
why_it_feels_right: Things at rest usually feel force-free, and zero speed sounds like nothing is happening.
why_wrong: Acceleration is the rate of change of velocity. At the end the spring is stretched most, so a = −ω²x is largest; velocity is zero for only an instant.
verify_flags: TODO_VERIFY
Concept-card worked example: ω = √(50/0.5) = 10 rad/s, v_max = ωA = 1 m/s, a_max = ω²A = 10 m/s², E = ½kA² = 0.25 J.

statement: Total mechanical energy stays the same throughout an ideal oscillation; only the KE/PE split changes.
wrong_idea: The energy is biggest in the middle where it moves fastest and drops at the ends.
why_it_feels_right: You can see the speed, so kinetic energy feels like all of the energy.
why_wrong: At the ends the kinetic energy has turned into potential energy, ½kx². With no damping nothing is lost, so KE + PE = ½kA² at every point.
verify_flags: TODO_VERIFY

statement: Each particle does SHM in place; the wave pattern moves at a speed set by the medium, not the source.
analogy: Stadium Mexican wave: fans only stand and sit, yet the wave runs round.
steps: Particles oscillate about their own mean positions
Pattern and energy pass from particle to particle
Medium sets speed: v = √(T/μ) on a string
Source sets f; amplitude leaves v unchanged
Hence λ = v/f

why_wrong: Each piece of the medium only moves up-down or back-forth about its own place. Only the pattern and energy move forward.

statement: Overlapping waves add displacements, then pass on unchanged; close frequencies beat at |f1 − f2|.
analogy: Like two queues crossing at a railway gate: they mix briefly, then walk on.
steps: Add displacements point by point while waves overlap.
Afterwards each wave keeps its shape and direction.
A flat string is still moving: energy is kinetic, not lost.
Beat rate = |f1 − f2|; heard pitch ≈ (f1 + f2)/2.
Fixed string: nodes λ/2 apart, fundamental = v/2L.
worked_example: Forks 256 Hz, 260 Hz: 4 beats per second, pitch ≈ 258 Hz.
verify_flags: TODO_VERIFY
Heard pitch = (f1 + f2)/2 is approximate and holds only for close frequencies
In beats, quiet moments redistribute sound energy in time; it is not destroyed (used in W4 beat-context options and probes)

statement: Cancellation is only momentary; the energy stays in the rope as motion and both pulses carry on.
wrong_idea: When the two pulses cancel, they destroy each other and the energy is gone.
why_it_feels_right: The rope looks completely flat, so it seems nothing is left.
why_wrong: Flat is not still. At that instant every bit of the rope is moving fast, so all the energy is kinetic. A moment later both pulses reappear.
verify_flags: TODO_VERIFY
Heard pitch = (f1 + f2)/2 is approximate and holds only for close frequencies
In beats, quiet moments redistribute sound energy in time; it is not destroyed (used in W4 beat-context options and probes)

statement: Pulses pass through each other and come out unchanged.
wrong_idea: The two pulses hit each other and bounce back like balls.
why_it_feels_right: Things we see colliding, like cricket balls or marbles, bounce off each other.
why_wrong: A pulse is not an object; it is a shape moving along the rope. Where two meet, displacements simply add. Send a tall and a short pulse: the tall one ends up at the far end.
verify_flags: TODO_VERIFY
Heard pitch = (f1 + f2)/2 is approximate and holds only for close frequencies
In beats, quiet moments redistribute sound energy in time; it is not destroyed (used in W4 beat-context options and probes)

statement: Beat frequency = |f1 − f2|.
wrong_idea: Beat frequency is f1 + f2, because both sounds play together.
why_it_feels_right: Superposition means adding, so adding the frequencies feels natural.
why_wrong: We add displacements, not frequencies. Loudness swells when the waves fall into step and fades when they fall out of step, which happens |f1 − f2| times per second. 440 Hz and 444 Hz give 4 beats, not 884.
verify_flags: TODO_VERIFY
Heard pitch = (f1 + f2)/2 is approximate and holds only for close frequencies
In beats, quiet moments redistribute sound energy in time; it is not destroyed (used in W4 beat-context options and probes)

statement: The average is the pitch; the beat rate is |f1 − f2|.
wrong_idea: The beat frequency is the average of the two frequencies.
why_it_feels_right: You really do hear a note near the average, so that number seems like the answer.
why_wrong: The average, (f1 + f2)/2, is the pitch you hear. The beat is how often the loudness throbs, which is the difference. 506 Hz and 512 Hz: pitch about 509 Hz, beats 6 per second.

statement: A plane mirror forms a virtual, erect, same-size image as far behind the mirror as you are in front.
analogy: Like a twin behind a window, copying your every step.
steps: Angle of incidence equals angle of reflection, from the normal
Image distance behind the mirror equals object distance in front
Step back and the image steps back too
So a full view needs a mirror half your height
worked_example: Sita, 1.5 m tall, stands 2 m away: image is 4 m from her; a 0.75 m mirror shows her fully.

statement: Light bends toward the normal entering a denser medium, away entering a rarer one; TIR needs denser-to-rarer travel beyond the critical angle.
analogy: A cycle rolling slantwise onto sand turns one way; back onto road, the other way.
steps: Compare n on both sides
Denser side: ray nearer the normal
Denser to rarer? sin C = n2/n1
TIR only if incidence angle exceeds C
worked_example: Glass to air, n = 1.5: sin C = 1/1.5, C ≈ 41.8°. At 45° inside: TIR. At 30°: exits at 48.6°.

statement: Waves from two slits add or cancel, giving fringes of width beta = lambda D / d; energy is only redistributed.
analogy: Like rearranging chairs: some rows fill, others empty, none added.
steps: Bright at path difference n lambda, dark at (n + 1/2) lambda
beta = lambda D / d
Smaller d gives wider fringes
Bright reaches 4I0, dark 0, average 2I0
Cover one slit and fringes vanish

statement: A smaller slit gap d gives wider fringes, since beta = lambda D / d.
wrong_idea: If the slits are closer, the fringes should be closer and thinner too.
why_it_feels_right: It seems the pattern should shrink with the slits, like a smaller stamp making a smaller print.
why_wrong: With closer slits the path difference grows more slowly along the screen, so you move farther to gain one wavelength. Hence beta = lambda D / d, which goes as 1/d.

statement: Interference redistributes light energy across the screen; it never creates or destroys it.
wrong_idea: Interference makes extra light at bright fringes and destroys light at dark ones.
why_it_feels_right: Bright fringes really are up to four times as bright as one slit alone, so light seems added.
why_wrong: Energy is conserved. Each slit gives I0, so 2I0 on average. Interference only moves energy: bright fringes reach 4I0, dark ones 0, and the average stays 2I0.

statement: A narrower slit gives a wider central maximum, and a tilted polaroid between crossed polaroids lets some light through.
analogy: Like a vertical gate then a horizontal gate: a slanted gate between lets some through.
steps: First minima: a sin θ = ±λ, so central width ≈ 2λD/a.
Smaller a, wider band.
Polaroid: I = I0 cos²θ; unpolarised gives I0/2.
Crossed pair plus 45° middle sheet: (I0/2)cos²45°cos²45° = I0/8.

why_wrong: When the slit is only a few wavelengths wide, light diffracts; the first minima sit at sin θ = λ/a, so a smaller a pushes them outward.

why_wrong: A polaroid also sets the direction of polarisation. Crossed polaroids give 0, but a 45° sheet between them turns the light so (I0/2)cos²45°cos²45° = I0/8 passes.
